title: Hosted API demo - Chat & text generation basics
summary: AE + SE demo of Redwood hosted API focusing on chat/text generation: streaming, key parameters (temperature, top_p, max_tokens), and retry/fallback behavior. Discussed integration patterns, costs, and next steps for pilot and security docs.
transcript:
Header: 2026-03-04 11:00AM PT | Duration: ~46m | Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Arjun Patel (Redwood SE), Jon Reyes (Summit Tech CTO), Priya Singh (PM), Liam O'Connor (SRE)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — Maya from Redwood, Arjun my SE is here too. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Jon: Good morning, thanks, all good. Jon here.
[00:07] Priya: Hi, Priya. Couple of other things on my side, excited to see the streaming bit.
[00:11] Arjun: Awesome. Quick agenda — I'll do a short console + API walkthrough showing chat and text generation basics: streaming, params, and then retries/fallbacks. We'll leave time for Q&A.
[00:19] Maya: Real quick, high level: Summit Tech told us you're prototyping an in-app assistant and need low latency for short queries and cheaper batch summarization. Is that still right?
[00:27] Jon: Yes. We have real-time chat for customers and nightly batch jobs for summarizing logs. Latency is a hard SLO for the chat path.
[00:33] Arjun: Perfect. I'll share my screen — console.redwood.ai/... (link shared)
[00:40] [00:40] Arjun: Starting in the Console: model catalog on left, we've got curated open models and some Redwood-verified performance profiles. For chat we usually recommend a mid-size variant for balancing cost and latency.
[00:55] Priya: Quick q, what's the difference between hosted and dedicated here?
[00:58] Maya: Hosted is our managed API — fastest to get going, usage-based. Dedicated is reserved capacity with guaranteed throughput and isolation if you need it. For prototyping hosted's usually fine.
[01:10] Arjun: Back to streaming. On the API we support chunked streaming for tokens. In code you'd open a streaming connection and get deltas as they generate. This reduces perceived latency for user-facing chat. Example snippet I show: client.chat.stream(..., {"stream": true, "temperature": 0.2, "max_tokens": 256}) — note: streaming requires handling partial deltas and finalization tokens.
[01:35] Liam: On the SRE side, how stable are the streaming connections? Any reconnect guidance?
[01:39] Arjun: Good question. We recommend exponential backoff and then a short window retry — if you don't get a final token you can re-issue the request with a prompt prefix of the last acknowledged tokens to avoid duplication. Our SDKs include helpers for streaming reconnects. There's also idempotency keys for non-streaming endpoints.
[01:56] Jon: How do you handle rate limits?
[01:58] Maya: We return standard 429s with a Retry-After header. For production we often set client-side token bucket to smooth spikes; Redwood Console also shows per-token usage and rate metrics so you can tune.
[02:12] [02:12] Arjun: Demo: toggling generation params. Temperature controls randomness — lower is more deterministic. Top_p is nucleus sampling — a different knob. We showed a pair of examples: temp 0.0 vs 0.8 for the same prompt, you can see the one with higher temp gives more varied phrasing.
[02:33] Priya: On summaries we'll want consistent output. So low temp?
[02:36] Arjun: Yes, for deterministic summarization set temperature 0-0.2 and consider a fixed max_tokens and stop sequences.
[02:44] [02:44] Maya: There's also a quality-vs-cost tradeoff: larger models produce higher quality but cost more per token. Redwood Optimize gives recommendations for quantization or swapping to a cheaper variant for batch jobs.
[02:58] Jon: Any auto-fallback if a model is out of capacity?
[03:01] Arjun: We do smart routing — if capacity constrained we can automatically fallback to a compatible model variant, based on your configured policy. You can set per-route fallbacks in Console (canary, a/b, fallback to cheaper).
[03:15] Liam: For data residency — is chat content retained? We need controls for logs/audit and retention.
[03:20] Maya: Hosted stores request logs for a configurable retention window; you can opt out of retention or enable encryption at rest with customer-managed KMS. For strict requirements, Private/VPC deployment is available. We'll share the SOC2 + security whitepaper.
[03:35] [03:35] Arjun: Now I'll show an API call from a dev machine. (shares code link) Example shows calling /v1/chat with messages array, temperature, top_p, max_tokens, and streaming true.
[03:50] [03:50] Arjun: Also demoing retries: we simulate a transient 500 and trigger the SDK retry logic. It retries with a backoff and respects idempotency. For streaming we use a resumed request pattern — client resumes from last saved token index.
[04:06] Priya: Are retries configurable per route?
[04:09] Arjun: Yes, in Console you can adjust retry policy per route — number of attempts, backoff base, and per-status behavior.
[04:16] [04:16] Jon: What about streaming + function calling? We saw other providers serialize function call payloads differently.
[04:22] Arjun: We support structured output and function/tool calling. Streaming function calls stream the arguments as they're generated, but function execution is local to the client once you decide to invoke. A few customers had to tweak parsing. There may be slight transcription hiccups: some docs refer to "function calling" as "tool calls" — sorry if I mix names.
[04:38] Maya: Real-world note: short-turn chat benefits the most from streaming — you get UX improvements without raising server-side concurrency much because tokens are emitted progressively.
[04:48] [04:48] Arjun: Quick perf note: we optimize KV cache and continuous batching at runtime. For long chats with KV cache reuse, you pay only for new tokens. There's also prefix caching for conversational systems.
[04:59] Liam: Curious about observability — what traces/metrics do we get?
[05:02] Maya: Console provides per-route latency percentiles, token counts, per-request traces (sampled), and error rates. You can export logs to your SIEM.
[05:12] Jon: Cost example for chat path?
[05:14] Maya: We ran a benchmark for a similar profile — short queries (avg 20 tokens) at 50 RPS — hosted cost estimate + latency numbers shared in the deck link. We'll send the spreadsheet with cost curves.
[05:27] [05:27] Arjun: Now I'll show code handling streaming in our Node SDK: open stream, on 'delta' append to UI, on 'done' finalize. We also show a pattern to handle partial outputs if a connection drops.
[05:42] Priya: Any guidance on stop sequences for multi-turn?
[05:44] Arjun: Use explicit stop tokens or sentinel phrases — also enforce max_tokens to avoid runaway. For chat, you can include system/user roles and then stop at role markers.
[05:55] [05:55] Jon: Security follow-up: can you share the SOC2 and data flow diagram?
[05:58] Maya: Yes, we'll attach those to the follow-up.
[06:02] Arjun: Troubleshooting: if you see truncated responses, check client buffer flush and make sure you handle partial chunking. Sometimes proxies (corporate) buffer streaming, so we recommend configuring chunked transfer encoding allowed in network.
[06:18] Liam: Good callout. We'll check our proxy.
[06:21] [06:21] Maya: Ok, quick recap before we close — next steps and owners.
[06:25] Jon: Sounds good.
[06:27] Priya: Couple of questions I'll email later about summarization edge cases.
[06:30] Maya: Perfect. Thanks everyone.

Note: transcription has occasional errors like "k v cache" for KV cache, and misattribution of speaker names in a few lines due to auto-transcription.

End of transcript.
